query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultrathin, pre‐sintering Cu‐coated graphene (Cu@Gr) interfacial layer on tungsten particles within a W–Cu composite will suppress phase separation and interfacial void formation under combined high heat‐flux and irradiation service conditions, thereby producing a composite with superior and irradiation‐stable thermal conductivity compared to an untreated composite.
generation.material_initial_state: A typical W–Cu composite in which tungsten exists as discrete particles or interconnected ligaments embedded in a copper matrix that, when processed by conventional sintering, displays phase separation and develops interfacial voids.
generation.intervention: Introduce an ultrathin Cu@Gr coating to the tungsten surfaces prior to sintering (by chemical plating or a similar controlled deposition technique) to modify the tungsten–copper interface during composite fabrication.
generation.conditions: Sintering at temperatures sufficient to achieve a liquid copper phase (e.g., near 1350 °C) with controlled time to prevent excessive copper evaporation, followed by service-simulated conditions that include high heat-transfer flux and irradiation (e.g., Ar+ or He+ fluences similar to those experienced at plasma-facing joint interfaces).
generation.structural_mediator: A conformal, nanoscale Cu@Gr interfacial layer that promotes improved copper wetting and continuous network formation while resisting void nucleation at tungsten–copper interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The Cu@Gr coating acts as a barrier that decreases the interfacial energy and inhibits copper evaporation and migration. By promoting enhanced wettability and interdiffusion control, it stabilizes the interface during high-temperature sintering and limits radiation-enhanced diffusion or void coalescence under irradiation, together preventing phase separation and interfacial void formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated composite is expected to exhibit a more uniform three-dimensional copper network with fewer interfacial voids, resulting in an improvement in thermal conductivity (potentially on the order of a 20–25% increase relative to untreated composites under identical high heat-flux and irradiation conditions) and enhanced stability of thermal performance during service.
generation.baseline: An untreated W–Cu composite processed under similar sintering conditions, which displays an increased propensity for phase separation and interfacial void formation leading to reductions in thermal conductivity under operating heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to composites produced by sintering processes where the copper phase is liquid (near the melting point of copper) but tungsten remains solid, and service conditions mimic those at the joints between plasma-facing tungsten components and copper-based cooling systems. It is particularly relevant when the processing parameters are optimized to form a continuous copper network without excessive copper evaporation.
generation.uncertainty: While results from PMC5736653 indicate that a small amount of Cu@Gr improves interfacial properties and thermal conductivity in WCu systems, and PMC12028711 highlights issues related to sintering time and resultant pore formation, the combined effect under irradiation has not been directly studied. The scale of improvement under irradiation and the robustness of the Cu@Gr layer against radiation-enhanced diffusion remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set with the ultrathin Cu@Gr coating applied to the tungsten particles and a control set without the coating. Process both by identical sintering protocols (e.g., temperature near 1350 °C with a carefully controlled short sintering time) and then subject them to accelerated thermal cycling and irradiation conditions (using Ar+ or He+ beams at fluences representative of joint service conditions).
measurements: Quantitative SEM/TEM analysis of interfacial void density and phase distribution before and after thermal/irradiation treatment.
Thermal conductivity measurements using laser flash analysis or equivalent methods before and after irradiation.
Density measurements and electrical conductivity as a complementary metric.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu@Gr-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in interfacial void density and fail to show improved or more stable thermal conductivity compared to the untreated control after both thermal cycling and irradiation, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 8 reveals the microstructure of W-20Cu composite after sintering the W-20Cu specimens at 1350 °C for 60, 120 and 180 min, respectively, where the grey tissue is the skeleton-like tungsten phase, and the light black tissue is the adherent phase copper at its periphery. A small number of tiny pores can be observed in Figure 8b1, and the copper phase is distributed in the interstices of tungsten particles. With the increasing sintering time, the pore size distribution first becomes more obvious and then decreases, which is due to the fact that in the process of high-temperature liquid-phase sintering, the wettability between the tungsten and copper is not very good at 1350 °C [,,,] and the liquid-phase copper will produce evaporation loss after generation. At the same time, due to the incomplete liquid-phase wettability, the interfacial energy of the solid–solid interface is lower than that of the solid–liquid interface, and solid particles come in contact with each other, making the copper melt permeation volume higher, so that the amount of copper melt penetration is reduced, part of the copper had to overflow. The important factors for densification by both solid state and liquid phase mechanisms are the two terms of solubility and diffusivity. For a conventional liquid phase sintering, the diffusivity of the base metal in the liquid is much larger than that along the grain boundary. For the case of WCu, the concentration of W in the liquid Cu is very small. As mentioned above, tungsten easily reacts with graphene, which can enhance activated sintering behavior. The grain boundary diffusivity is substantially increased due to the presence of the activator (i.e. graphene) and enhanced volume (or mass) transport of W. In addition, formation of a continuous Cu network, achievement of a high relative density of composites and successful integration of graphene into the WCu composites are the other key reasons for the good thermal and electrical properties of WCu composites obtained in this work.
